items.content:
I hit 200,000 followers.

I joined X in September 2024, so it took me a little under two years to get here.

Honestly, the past few days have been rough for me.

Someone tried to dig up my personal information, managed to identify some of it, and spread it around.

Lately, whenever I see new replies, I have not always had the courage to read them. I have been afraid of what kind of abuse might be waiting there.

But I also looked through the replies to some of the posts mocking me for my age, and people’s perception of me was much kinder than I had expected. It made me feel proud that I may have contributed something worthwhile to this community and conducted myself reasonably well along the way.

I have also received many encouraging messages in my DMs. I am deeply grateful for them.
I would like to clear up a couple of misunderstandings.

1. Jukan bought 2x leveraged SK Hynix at the top in June?

No. I have held a memory position since January, and the part about buying leveraged Hynix in June was a joke. I do not have the guts to run leverage, and my boss and I make jokes like that sometimes. I had no idea that making that kind of joke publicly would bring this much mockery down on me.

2. Is Jukan merely pretending to be an analyst while doing nothing more than quoting other analysts and news reports?

If you have mostly seen my posts on X, I can understand why you might feel that way. But you can find more of my original research and analysis in Citrini’s institutional reports and on our Substack.

Because I work for a firm, there are limits to how much of that work I can share publicly on X. I hope people can understand that.

As for why I appeared to change my view on memory, I said at the time that my long-term thesis had not changed. Still, many people seem to have interpreted my comments as me turning bearish on memory altogether. That was not my intention, although I accept that I could have expressed myself more clearly.

At that time, with HBM content getting nerfed, I thought that even though this was clearly a supply problem and not a demand problem, people would take it bearishly, so memory stocks could perform poorly from a trading perspective. That is why I wrote what I wrote. But it snowballed into something far bigger than I intended.

If I could go back to that moment, I would not write that post.

Watching people I have never met at all hurl abuse at me is more painful than I expected. I used to think of being an influencer as something trivial, but it turns out to be harder than I ever imagined.

This ended up being a more vulnerable post than I intended.

But I got here because of all of you who have read, shared, and supported my work.

Thank you.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 14, 2026

items.content:
《GF Securities Overseas Electronics Newsletter》 

☄ Intel (INTC, Buy): Equity Offering Signals Confidence, Foundry and EMIB Continue to Advance

☀ Reiterate Buy and $136 target price: We view this equity offering as sending a positive signal. The CEO’s direct subscription demonstrates confidence, and it also reflects the smooth progress of the foundry business. We expect the foundry business to reach breakeven (BEP) in 4Q27, with margin leverage kicking in fully in 2028. Yields and external customer acquisition (particularly Apple) are progressing solidly, and the EMIB customer base is also expanding (Google and AWS). Intel has secured support from substrate (carrier) supplier Unimicron, and will produce silicon capacitors internally. We raise our 2026E/2027E EPS estimates by 3%/1% respectively and maintain our $136 target price, factoring in dilution.

☀ The equity offering sends a positive signal: Intel upsized the offering from an initial $15bn to $20bn, and institutional demand reportedly exceeded $100bn. The offering price was $95, and the overallotment option (greenshoe) was fully exercised. CEO Lip-Bu Tan and his family subscribed for roughly $12mn at the offering price, which we read as a signal of management’s confidence in the company, and which should also support FY27 capex.

☀ A solid EMIB customer base drives the foundry business further: Intel reaffirmed its guidance that the foundry business will reach breakeven by the end of 2027, and stated that if this slips to 2028 it would mainly be due to increased new investment requirements. We maintain our existing view that 2Q26 18A yields are around 80%, and CWF (Clearwater Forest) has already entered the production ramp phase. Collaboration with external customers also continues to progress, with Apple’s 14A high volume production particularly notable. We raise our FY27/FY28 backend revenue estimates to $1.1bn/$7.0bn respectively, driven by improved visibility on AWS Trainium3 (T3) adopting EMIB-T in 2027, and by Google’s Humufish/Triggerfish entering volume expansion in 2H27 to 2028. We also expect ASICs from AWS and Microsoft could adopt EMIB in 2028.

 $INTC

Taiwan's DigiTimes reports that Nvidia's Feynman platform, the generation after next, will move straight to A16, TSMC's upgraded version of its 2nm process, and will also raise the share of SoIC 3D stacking, with custom HBM and CPO expected to be combined on top of that.

Accordingly, TSMC's monthly SoIC capacity is said to reach 50,000 wafers a month by the end of 2027.

What is also interesting is that AP7 P2, which was planned for SoIC, may be partly allocated to CPO and CoWoS lines. This could mean CPO is being pulled forward earlier than expected.

ASE's subsidiary SPIL is also said to be establishing itself as a key vendor winning Nvidia orders. This stems from the fact that even if TSMC expands capacity at full force, it will be difficult to meet all customer demand.

items.content:
GF Securities Overseas Electronics and Communications: CoreWeave 2Q26 Earnings Comment

Maintaining Buy rating and $172 target price: CoreWeave posted 2Q26 revenue of $2.6 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $1.5 billion, both above consensus. The company currently operates 1.5GW of compute power, and contracted capacity stands at 4.2GW, keeping it on track toward its 8GW target for 2030. Management guided to midpoints of $230 million for 3Q26 adjusted operating income and $1,055 million for full year 2026. That implies 4Q26 operating income of roughly $770 million at the top end of guidance, pointing to a very strong fourth quarter.

We remain positive on CoreWeave for the following reasons. 1) With AI infrastructure demand strong and cash flow pressure building at the major cloud operators, the market for emerging cloud service providers continues to expand. 2) Pricing power keeps strengthening, and the company raised prices across all products by 25% starting in July. 3) The backlog stands at $129 billion, giving very high earnings visibility. 4) The launch of the DDTL 5.5 financing structure has made financing available even for contracts as short as three years. Shorter contracts generally carry higher prices.

The company raised its 2026 capex guidance to $35 billion to $39 billion, but the 2Q26 EBITDA improvement and continued power capacity expansion have eased market concerns to some degree. We forecast revenue of $12.7 billion, $27.3 billion and $41.8 billion for 2026, 2027 and 2028, and adjusted EBITDA of $7.5 billion, $15.6 billion and $21.2 billion. Our $172 target price is unchanged and is derived by applying 10x 2028 estimated EV/EBITDA.

A direct beneficiary of the expanding emerging cloud market: The market is concerned that the entry of new players such as Meta and SpaceX will intensify competition and disperse demand. We judge, however, that the current buildout plans of these players are not enough to resolve the structural shortage of compute resources. More importantly, the long term take-or-pay contracts CoreWeave signs offer greater revenue stability than on demand rentals or short term contracts. The company's total operating costs are also up to 47% lower than the average hyperscaler, giving it a clear edge in cost and operating efficiency.

The path to margin improvement is on track as well.

1. As we noted in our initiation report, new bookings are capturing the full benefit of higher GPU rental rates. According to management, margins on 2Q26 new contracts are 5 to 10 percentage points higher than on existing contracts. On top of that, with the 25% across the board price increase in July, the $25 billion of new contracts to be signed in 3Q26 will carry even higher pricing.

2. The model of continuing to monetize assets after contracts expire is delivering. Some A100 GPUs deployed in 2020 are already contracted out through 2029.

3. The push into the Asia Pacific market is also accelerating. The company has secured 360MW of compute capacity in Indonesia, where low local data center operating costs should further improve profitability.

 $CRWV 
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 13, 2026
